description.summary: A composite chimera-like creature originating in Chinese mythology (mò 貘) and adopted into Japanese folklore (baku 獏) by the Muromachi period, traditionally invoked to consume nightmares and protect sleepers. The same Sino-Japanese word now also denotes the tapir.
description.full: Baku (獏 / 貘) is a chimerical supernatural creature whose roots lie in Chinese mythology — where it is called mò (貘) — and which was incorporated into Japanese folklore by the Muromachi period (1336-1573). Surviving Edo-period encyclopaedic works such as Terajima Ryōan's Wakan Sansai Zue (1712) describe it as a composite beast: typically with the trunk and tusks of an elephant, the eyes of a rhinoceros, the tail of an ox, and the paws of a tiger; later Japanese illustrations emphasise the elephantine head. The baku is most strongly associated with the consumption of nightmares (akumu 悪夢). A common Japanese ritual practice on waking from a bad dream is to call out 'Baku-san, come eat my dream' (獏さん、夢を食べてください, baku-san, yume wo tabete kudasai); some traditions warn that excessive invocation can lead the creature to consume good dreams and aspirations as well. Pictures and small figures of the baku were placed on or near pillows as protective talismans, especially in the Edo period and continuing into modern Japan. From the 17th century onward, when Dutch traders introduced Southeast Asian Malayan tapirs (Tapirus indicus) to Japan, the visual resemblance — particularly the elongated snout and pied colouring — led to the same word baku being used for the real animal, conflating the two in modern Japanese usage.

etymology.origin: Chinese 貘 (mò), describing an ancient Chinese mythological beast; transmitted to Japan as 獏 (baku) by the Muromachi period.
etymology.meaning: In its original mythological sense, the name denoted the supernatural creature; in modern Japanese it is also used for the biological tapir (Tapirus spp.).
etymology.first_use: Chinese references date back at least to early dictionaries such as the Erya (3rd century BCE-2nd century CE); in Japan, well attested from the Muromachi period and especially the Edo period.

related_phenomena.name: Bai Ze (Hakutaku)
related_phenomena.description: Another protective composite Sino-Japanese mythological creature.

related_phenomena.name: Tapir (Tapirus spp.)
related_phenomena.description: Real animal that came to share the name baku in Japanese usage from the 17th century onward.

features.description: Most descriptions place an elephant's trunk and tusks at the front of the creature.
Edo encyclopaedias variously give it the eyes of a rhinoceros or the ears of a rhinoceros.
An ox's tail is the standard tail attribution.
Tiger or feline paws are a recurring component.
Some early descriptions give it the body of a bear.

physical.morphology: A composite chimera. The most frequent canonical description in Japan (after Wakan Sansai Zue, 1712, and other Edo references) gives it an elephant's trunk and tusks, a rhinoceros's eyes, an ox's tail, and a tiger's paws.

abilities.description: Consumes bad dreams when summoned by a sleeper, preventing them from manifesting as misfortune.
In its original Chinese context the creature wards off evil spirits and pestilence.
Pictures and figurines of the baku placed near a pillow are believed to bring restful sleep.

patterns: Approached as a benevolent guardian rather than a danger
Invoked specifically on waking from nightmares
Linked to bedside objects: pillow-prints, talismans, netsuke

range.description: Originating in Chinese mythological tradition (mò 貘) and adopted into Japanese folklore by the Muromachi period; later transmitted across the Sinosphere and globally via popular culture.

first_recorded.source: Chinese textual references to mò (貘); the Erya and later Han dynasty sources mention the creature.

peak_activity_periods.description: Adoption of the figure into Japanese culture via Buddhist and literary transmission.
Peak popularity of baku imagery on bedding, pillows, woodblock prints, and netsuke; Wakan Sansai Zue (1712) codifies the description.

origins.cultural_roots: Chinese mythological beast (mò 貘), associated with auspiciousness and protection from pestilence. Transmitted to Japan via Buddhist and literary channels in the Muromachi period.
origins.earliest_accounts: Chinese: Han-era dictionaries and bestiaries reference mò. Japanese: Muromachi-period adoption, with major Edo-period documentation in Wakan Sansai Zue (1712) and various ukiyo-e and pillow-print traditions.
origins.folklore_connections: Linked to other Sino-Japanese composite auspicious beasts (qilin, bai ze) and to the Japanese tradition of bedside protective talismans.

timeline.event: Chinese textual references describe mò (貘) as an auspicious/protective creature.
Baku enters Japanese folklore via Buddhist/literary transmission from China.
timeline.source: Secondary scholarship on Sino-Japanese cultural transmission.

timeline.event: Terajima Ryōan publishes Wakan Sansai Zue (和漢三才図会), an Edo-era encyclopaedia, with an illustrated entry on baku.
Dutch traders bring Southeast Asian Malayan tapirs to Japan; their resemblance to baku imagery leads to shared naming.
timeline.significance: Origin of the modern Japanese conflation between baku-the-yokai and baku-the-tapir.

timeline.event: Baku images appear on pillows, bedding, ukiyo-e prints, and netsuke as protective talismans.

history.modern_era: In modern Japan, baku continues as a benign figure in popular culture, associated with peaceful sleep and protection from nightmares. The same word is also the standard Japanese term for the biological tapir, and the two are commonly conflated in children's media and zoological education.

documentary.name: Wakan Sansai Zue (和漢三才図会)
documentary.description: Edo-period Japanese encyclopaedia compiled by Terajima Ryōan, with an illustrated entry on baku as a composite mythical beast.

documentary.name: Edo-period baku pillow prints and netsuke
documentary.description: Edo-period bedside protective imagery and small carvings depicting baku, used to ward off nightmares.
documentary.source: Edo-era decorative arts; museum collections (e.g. British Museum, Tokyo National Museum).

paranormal.name: Genuine dream-eating yōkai / mythical beast
paranormal.description: Within Chinese and Japanese tradition, the baku is treated as a real supernatural creature that can be invoked from one's bedside to consume nightmares.

skeptical.name: Cultural invention / iconographic confusion
skeptical.description: The baku is a longstanding mythological figure with no zoological reality; the modern conflation with tapir reflects 17th-century iconographic resemblance rather than any natural basis for the dream-eater belief.
evidence_cited: Documented Edo encounters with imported Malayan tapirs

traditions: Chinese mythological tradition of auspicious composite beasts
stories: Children's-book and modern-anime stories of baku eating bad dreams
folklore.beliefs: A bedside image or invocation of the baku is widely held to bring restful sleep and consume nightmares. Some traditions warn that over-invocation can lead the creature to devour good dreams and ambitions as well.

literature: Lafcadio Hearn, Kwaidan and other Japanese-folklore essays (1900s)
Michael Dylan Foster, The Book of Yōkai (UC Press, 2015)
film_tv: Numerous appearances in Japanese anime and manga
Pokémon — Drowzee/Hypnos line is widely identified by Game Freak as inspired by baku imagery
games: Shin Megami Tensei series — Baku appears as a recurring demon
other: Children's bedtime imagery, pajamas, and bedding in modern Japan continue to use baku motifs
